UPDATE: Kimberley Sewage Crisis

By: Ofentse Lamola | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
A year after Carte Blanche exposed Kimberley’s sewage crisis, the SA Human Rights Commission has now recommended that Sol Plaatje’s sanitation collapse be declared a provincial disaster. But for r

Unique Selling Point:
Carte Blanche first showed the broken promises and sewage failures in Kimberley and the wider Northern Cape. Now, the SAHRC has formally found that Sol Plaatje Municipality’s sewage and sanitation crisis is severe, prolonged and widespread enough to warrant a provincial disaster declaration. This update asks what happens next, and whether the people living with the consequences will finally see action.

Summary:
In May 2024, Carte Blanche investigated broken promises across the Northern Cape, including failed infrastructure, unfinished public projects, sewage problems and communities who said they had been abandoned by government. The insert included Kimberley’s collapsing water and sewage infrastructure, with sewage running through streets and concerns over public money spent without visible improvement.

In November 2025, Carte Blanche returned to Kimberley for the 1 Billion Rand Housing update. The insert revisited Nellie Frans in Roodepan, who had been waiting decades for a proper home after government promised a R1 billion housing project, a school and a hospital. The same insert also moved into the wider Sol Plaatje sewage crisis, including Platfontein, the Goga pump station, and the sewage lake affecting the Khwe community.

Carte Blanche found that Platfontein did not have a sewage network, yet sewage from elsewhere was flowing into or near the community’s land. The previous insert also showed the Goga pump station being switched on while the crew was filming, only to be switched off again shortly afterwards, with sewage continuing to overflow into the environment.

The new development is the release of the SAHRC inquiry report into service delivery failures in the Northern Cape. The report recommends that Premier Zamani Saul declare a provincial disaster in relation to sewage spillages and associated sanitation failures in Sol Plaatje Municipality. The update will ask what practical intervention should follow, who is responsible for implementation, and what residents can expect within the next six months.

Further information:
The 2024 Broken Promises: Northern Cape insert positioned the province as a place of unfinished projects and failed government commitments. It looked at Kimberley’s water collapse, Hopetown’s incomplete electrification and stadium projects, Philipstown’s abandoned housing infrastructure, and other failed public works. The proposal noted that Kimberley’s water infrastructure had been neglected for more than 20 years and that two wastewater treatment plants were completely rundown.

The 2025 1 Billion Rand Housing update began with Nellie Frans and the failed housing promise, but the insert’s strongest current relevance is the Sol Plaatje sewage crisis. It showed Platfontein, where the Khwe community lives near a sewage lake, and where residents said they do not receive proper services. Markus Jetembo questioned why a community without proper services or flush toilets should have sewage dumped on its land.

The earlier Flamingo Rescue insert from 2019 is relevant as background because it linked the drying up of Kamfers Dam to the failure of the Homevale Wastewater Treatment Plant and broader municipal sewage infrastructure. The insert explained that Kamfers Dam relies on treated effluent from Homevale, but that because the plant was not functioning properly, raw effluent was instead flowing into nearby wetlands and veld.

For this update, however, the flamingo angle should remain secondary unless needed for context. The strongest 4-minute version is the human rights and accountability angle: the crisis Carte Blanche previously showed on the ground has now been formally recognised by the SAHRC.

Kimberley Sewage Crisis: Disaster on Paper, Sewage on the Ground

When Carte Blanche was last in Kimberley, residents were living with sewage in their streets, homes and communities. In Platfontein, an indigenous Khwe community without proper sanitation services was living near a growing sewage lake. In Roodepan and other parts of Sol Plaatje, residents said they had been complaining for years, with little visible change.

Now, the South African Human Rights Commission has released its inquiry report into service delivery failures in the Northern Cape, recommending that Premier Zamani Saul declare a provincial disaster in relation to sewage spillages and associated sanitation failures in Sol Plaatje Municipality.

The Commission found that the crisis is severe, prolonged and widespread, with sanitation failures affecting residents’ health, dignity, homes and environment. It also found that the municipality lacks the technical and financial capacity to manage the crisis alone.

In this update, Carte Blanche returns to the Sol Plaatje sewage crisis to ask what happens now. Will the SAHRC’s recommendations trigger real intervention, emergency support and accountability? Or will residents continue to live with the consequences while government promises another plan?
With affected residents, local voices and the SAHRC, Carte Blanche asks whether this report will finally bring action, or become another document in a province already scarred by broken promises.
